facts.claim: "Spectre" is a song by the English rock band Radiohead. It was produced by Nigel Godrich.
Radiohead recorded "Spectre", an orchestral ballad, for the 2015 James Bond film Spectre after their earlier submission "Man of War" was rejected.
Radiohead released "Spectre" as a free download on SoundCloud on Christmas Day 2015. It was their first release since the 2011 single "The Daily Mail" / "Staircase".
Thom Yorke said on Twitter that the band was asked to write a tune for the Bond movie Spectre and that it "didn't work out". He posted a clip of the track as the year closed.
Jonny Greenwood said the song was rejected for being "too dark". Sam Smith's "Writing's on the Wall" became the film's theme.
Nigel Godrich called the Bond experience a "real waste of energy" that disrupted work on A Moon Shaped Pool.
The song opens with minor piano chords over strings and synthesisers, and Yorke sings in falsetto.
Pitchfork named "Spectre" Best New Music. It called the song one of the finest Radiohead songs in some years.
"Spectre" appeared as a B-side on the vinyl single of "Burn the Witch".

Radiohead's Bond work interrupted sessions for A Moon Shaped Pool, which was produced by Nigel Godrich. That album's strings and choir were arranged by Jonny Greenwood and played by the London Contemporary Orchestra.

research.lineage: The song sits in the tradition of orchestral Bond-theme ballads. Sources say it has a sombre, sweeping grandeur that "might have fit well into the Bond song canon", and it comes out of the string-and-piano work Radiohead did around A Moon Shaped Pool.

draft:
The first thing Thom Yorke sings on **Spectre** is a confession, not a threat: "I'm lost, I'm a ghost." There's no swagger in it. It comes in falsetto, high and breathy, each note held long while the melody barely moves, circling a few pitches like someone pacing a small room. Underneath, minor piano chords roll out in slow arpeggios. Then the strings come in and start to breathe, swelling and pulling back. There are no drums. Nothing pushes the song forward. It just hangs in the air.

That stillness is part of why it never became a Bond theme. Radiohead wrote it for the 2015 film after an earlier try, "Man of War," was turned down, and this one didn't make it either. Jonny Greenwood said it was rejected for being "too dark," and Sam Smith's "Writing's on the Wall" took the slot. Nigel Godrich, who produced it, later called the whole episode a "real waste of energy" that cut into work on A Moon Shaped Pool. The band gave the song away on SoundCloud on Christmas Day, their first new music since 2011, and Pitchfork called it one of their finest songs in years.

The darkness Greenwood mentioned lives less in the arrangement than in where the song stands. The big orchestral Bond ballad usually sings about danger from a safe height. This one sings from inside it. The narrator is emptied out and occupied by something else, with a hunger that burns through like a bullet. Rumour, suspicion, anger and fear pile up like symptoms. Against all of that there's exactly one solid thing, a kiss: "Is when you put your lips to me." It's the tenderest line here and the shakiest one, because a few lines later fear has the narrator second-guessing even love.

Watch what happens when the lines come back. They return almost word for word, but "could see" turns into "can see." Where the lover's lips used to be, the answer is now "Spectre has come for me." The one truth has changed hands. Love was what the narrator held onto. By the last line, the only sure thing left is the thing that's hunting them. Yorke doesn't raise his voice for it. The doubled vocal stays soft, and the strings keep rising and falling, as if the narrator had known all along this was coming.

That calm is where the grief sits. A rejected spy theme turns out to be a quiet song about losing your grip on the one person who made sense, and it holds you there with the narrator, unafraid and undone at once, as the dark finally arrives.
